lessons.title: Running notebook cells in order
lessons.goal: Run cells in order and understand what Python keeps in memory.
lessons.body:
The Python kernel keeps the variables created when cells are run. Editing the text of a cell does not change the variable in memory: you must run that cell again.

The two cells deliberately use a simple calculation so that you can focus on the order of execution rather than the difficulty of the calculation.
codeCells: print(a*2)
lessons.code:
a=3

print(a*2)
cellLabels: Use the value currently in memory

practice.task: Run cell 1 and then cell 2. Next, replace a=3 with a=5 without running cell 1, and run cell 2 again. Finally, run cells 1 and 2 in order.
practice.expected: The result stays at 6 until the new assignment has been executed. It then becomes 10. Restarting clears the variables: run the cells again in order.

lessons.title: Python as a calculator
lessons.goal: Perform arithmetic operations and calculate a power.
lessons.body: A cell can evaluate an expression. Python displays the result of the last expression in the cell. The operators + and * perform addition and multiplication; ** denotes a power.

lessons.title: Data types
lessons.goal: Identify numbers, strings and Boolean values.
lessons.body:
The type function tells you the type of a value: int for an integer, float for a floating-point number, str for a string, and bool for a Boolean value.

Quotation marks delimit a string. They therefore change the meaning of a value such as 2.
lessons.code:
type(2)

type(2.5)

type('Bonjour tous le monde')

type(True)

practice.expected: Without quotation marks, 2 is an integer; with quotation marks, "2" is a string.

lessons.title: Print, comments and variables
lessons.goal: Store a value, comment on a calculation and display its result.
lessons.body:
print displays a value or text. The = sign assigns a value to a variable name. The # character introduces a comment: Python ignores everything that follows it on that line.

The second example calculates the energy of a photon using E = hc/λ. Here, the name l represents the wavelength in metres. The units must be consistent to obtain an energy in joules.
lessons.code:
# Premier programme Python

c = 299792456.2 # vitesse de la lumière en m/s
l = 600e-9 # exprimé en m soit une longueur d'onde de 600nm
E = h*c/l
print(E,'J')

lessons.title: Lists
lessons.goal: Create a list and select its elements.
lessons.body:
A list uses square brackets and can contain several data types. Its indices start at 0; a negative index counts from the end.

In L1[start:stop:step], the stop index is excluded. L1[::2] selects every other element. The + operator concatenates two lists: it does not add their elements together individually.

print(L1[2:-2]) #valeurs de la troisième position à la position -2 exclue
print(L1[2::3]) #valeurs données à partir de la troisième position avec un pas de 3

lessons.title: Modifying a list
lessons.goal: Add, change and remove elements.
lessons.body:
A list is mutable: you can replace a value by assignment, add an element with append or insert, and remove elements with remove or pop.

append adds to the end; insert takes a position. remove looks for a value; pop takes an index. Here, each cell recreates its starting list.
lessons.code:
# on modifie la donnée en troisième position
a=3
L1=[a,2.5,'bleu']
L1[2]=5
print(L1)

a=3
L1=[a,2.5,'bleu']
L1.append('rouge') # on ajoute la donnée 'rouge' en fin de liste
print(L1)
L1.insert(1,'rouge') # on ajoute la donnée 'rouge' en deuxième position
print(L1)

a=3
L1=[a,2.5,'bleu','rouge']
L1.remove('rouge') # on supprime la donnée 'rouge'
print(L1)
L1.pop(1) # on supprime la donnée en deuxième position
print(L1)

A tuple is a sequence whose elements cannot be reassigned as they can in a list. The example uses parentheses to create T1.

A dictionary associates keys with values. Here, the keys "H", "C" and "O" provide access to molar masses. The keys() and values() methods let you inspect this structure. The last cell adds the key "N".

lessons.title: Defining and using a function
lessons.goal: Define a function and reuse a calculation.
lessons.body:
def defines a function. The parameters in parentheses receive the values passed when the function is called. The indented instructions form the body of the function; return returns the result.

The first function calculates a square. The second reuses the relationship VM = RT/p for two sets of temperature and pressure values. Temperature is in kelvins and pressure in pascals; the factor of 1 000 converts m3·mol−1 into L·mol−1.
lessons.code:
def function(x):
    y=x**2
    return y
print(type(function))
print(function(2))

#On définit une fonction permettant de calculer le volume molaire d'un gaz parfait
def volume_molaire(T,p):
    R=8.314
    V_M=R*T/p*1000 #multiplier par 1000 permet d'avoir le résultat non pas en m3/mol mais en L/mol
    return V_M
#calcul du volume molaire dans les conditions normales de température et de pression
print('V_M dans les CNTP',volume_molaire(273.15,1.013e5),'L/mol')
#calcul du volume molaire dans les conditions standard de température et de pression
print('V_M dans les CSTP',volume_molaire(293.15,1e5),'L/mol')

lessons.title: Conditional statements
lessons.goal: Choose which instructions to execute according to a condition.
lessons.body:
if, elif and else select a block according to a condition. Only one branch is executed. Indentation delimits each block.

The deg2 function handles the three cases for the discriminant Δ: positive, zero or negative. Equality is tested with ==; = assigns a value. Here, a is assumed to be nonzero.
lessons.code:
# Résolution d'une équation du second degré
def deg2(a,b,c):
    delta=b**2-4*a*c # on définit ici le calcul du discriminant
    if delta>0: # cas où le discriminant est positif
        d=delta**0.5
        x1=(-b+d)/(2*a)
        x2=(-b-d)/(2*a)
        return ['x1=',x1,'x2=',x2]
    elif delta==0: # cas où le discriminant est nul. Il est important de mettre == et non =.
# Le == permet de comparer deux valeurs alors que le = affecte une valeur à une variable
        return [-b/(2*a)]
    else:
        return ["l'équation n'a pas de solution réelle"]
print (deg2(1,10**-7.5,-10**-9.5))

# Essais complémentaires des trois branches
print(deg2(1,-3,2))
print(deg2(1,-2,1))
print(deg2(1,0,1))

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.goal: Repeat a calculation with for and while.
lessons.body:
for iterates over the values provided by range(start, stop, step). The stop value is excluded and the arguments to range are integers.

while repeats its block as long as the condition is true. The condition is tested before each iteration. An instruction in the block must allow this condition to change, to avoid an infinite loop.
lessons.code:
for i in range (0,10,2):
    a=i
    print(i)

a=2
while a<=8:
    a=3*a
    print(a)

lessons.title: Modules
lessons.goal: Import a function or a library.
lessons.body:
Libraries bring together reusable functions. The scientific libraries used in this course are available in Basthon: you only need to import them.

from math import log10 lets you call log10 directly. import numpy as np gives the module a short name, so you write np.log10. This explicit access avoids confusion between functions with the same name.
lessons.code:
from math import log10
a=log10(0.1)
print(a)

import numpy as np
a=np.log10(0.1)
print(a)

lessons.title: Creating NumPy arrays
lessons.goal: Build an array and a sequence of values.
lessons.body:
np.array builds an array from explicitly specified values. np.arange defines a sequence using a step size and excludes the stop value. np.linspace defines a sequence using a number of points and, by default, includes both endpoints.

A NumPy array has a common data type and supports operations on all its values. Here, type(a) identifies the object as an ndarray.

print(a)

min and max return values; argmin and argmax return their indices.

reshape(3,2) arranges the six elements of the second array into three rows and two columns. The total number of elements must stay the same.

lessons.title: Calculating a numerical derivative
lessons.goal: Estimate a derivative while accounting for the x-coordinates.
lessons.body:
np.gradient(y,x) estimates dy/dx from the points in the array. The second argument supplies the x-coordinates: without it, the spacing is assumed to be 1.

For y = x2, the analytical derivative is 2x. The code plots both results to compare the numerical calculation with the known value. In TP2, the same method gives dpH/dVB.
codeCells:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(0,10,100)
y=x**2
dy_dx=np.gradient(y,x)
plt.plot(x,dy_dx,label='Dérivée numérique')
plt.plot(x,2*x,'--',label='Dérivée analytique')
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('dy/dx')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

lessons.title: Random numbers
lessons.goal: Generate random values and describe their distribution.
lessons.body:
np.random.randint(1,10,20) draws twenty integers from 1 inclusive to 10 exclusive. In this example, the resulting array is added to a list: the list therefore contains one array, rather than twenty separate elements.

np.random.normal(mu,sigma,N) generates N values from a normal distribution. mean() and std() calculate the mean and standard deviation of the generated values. Results vary from one draw to the next.

m=a.mean()
s=a.std()
print(f'mu = {m:.2f}','\t',f'sigma = {s:.2f}')

lessons.title: Plotting a curve
lessons.goal: Plot a function and label its axes.
lessons.body:
plt.plot plots the values of the function ln(x). We start at x=0.1 because the real logarithm is only defined for strictly positive x.

label gives the plot a name; legend() displays it. The xlabel, ylabel and title commands label the axes and the figure. show() requests the display.
lessons.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(0.1,100,10000)
def f(x):
    return np.log(x)
plt.plot(x,f(x),label='y=ln(x)')
plt.legend()
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('y')
plt.title('Représentation graphique de la fonction ln(x)')
plt.show()

lessons.title: Plotting a histogram
lessons.goal: Display a distribution of values.
lessons.body:
A histogram counts observations in intervals called bins. The code generates 10 000 values with a theoretical mean of 10 and a standard deviation of 0.5.

bins sets the number of bins within the interval selected by range. edgecolor and color set the outline and fill colours. Here, the vertical axis represents a count, not a probability density.
lessons.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.random.normal(10,0.5,10000)
plt.hist(x,bins=100,range=(0,20),edgecolor='k',color='grey')
plt.xlabel('Valeur')
plt.ylabel('Effectif')
plt.title('Distribution normale de moyenne 10 et d’écart-type 0,5')
plt.show()

lessons.goal: Display the proportions of a mixture.
lessons.body:
The three lists associate gas names, volume fractions and colours. Elements at the same position in these lists correspond to one another.

plt.pie displays the proportions. Small fractions can produce closely spaced labels: a pie chart shows the major components clearly, but is less effective at distinguishing trace components.
lessons.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
elements=['$N_2$','$O_2$','Ar','$CO_2$']
composition=[78.084,20.946,0.934,0.037]
couleurs=['blue','lightcoral','gold','green']
plt.pie(composition,labels=elements,colors=couleurs)
plt.show()

lessons.title: Polynomial regression
lessons.goal: Fit a polynomial to data.
lessons.body:
The code builds data following y = x2 − 3.2x + 1.8, then fits a degree-2 polynomial using np.polyfit.

The coefficients in mod are ordered from the highest power to the constant term. The ymodel line reconstructs the polynomial. The points are labelled “experimental” in the example, but they are actually simulated data without noise.
lessons.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x=np.linspace(0,50,100)
y=x**2-3.2*x+1.8
plt.scatter(x,y,color='black',label='experimental')
plt.legend()
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('f(x)')


mod=np.polyfit(x,y,2)
print(mod)

ymodel=mod[0]*(x**2)+mod[1]*x+mod[2]
plt.plot(x,ymodel,color='red',label='modelisation')
plt.legend()

plt.show()

lessons.title: Linear regression
lessons.goal: Determine a best-fit straight line and its parameters.
lessons.body:
Here, the data are simulated using y = 4x + 2. linregress calculates the slope and intercept. The code accesses them through regression[0] and regression[1].

The result also has the attributes slope, intercept, rvalue, pvalue, stderr and intercept_stderr. The coefficient of determination R2 is the square of rvalue. The legacy unpacking behaviour returns five values, even though the object exposes these six attributes.
lessons.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import linregress

x=np.linspace(0,50,100)
y=4*x+2
plt.scatter(x,y,color='black',label='experimental')
plt.legend()
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('f(x)')


regression=linregress(x,y)
ymodel = regression[0]*x+regression[1]
plt.plot(x,ymodel,color='red',label='modelisation')
plt.legend()

print(regression)

lessons.body:
The code builds a NumPy array of nine values arranged in three rows and three columns, then converts it to a Pandas DataFrame.

index names the rows and columns names the columns. The DataFrame display lets you locate a value by its label rather than its position alone. Reading files is covered in the next activity.

lessons.title: Reading a CSV and selecting data
lessons.goal: Import a file, inspect its columns and select data.
lessons.body:
The first cell prepares a small practice file. The second reads it using pd.read_csv, inspects its contents and selects a column, then some rows.

df.head() displays the first few rows; df.columns displays the exact column names. The filter df["temperature_C"]>22 keeps the rows that satisfy the condition.

Here, the separator is a comma. For a file separated by semicolons, use sep=";". The TP3 files use commas.
codeCells:
# Préparation du fichier d’entraînement
with open('mesures_exemple.csv','w',encoding='utf-8') as fichier:
    fichier.write('temps_s,temperature_C
0,20.0
10,22.5
20,24.0
')

import pandas as pd
df=pd.read_csv('mesures_exemple.csv')
print(df.head())
print(df.columns)
print(df['temperature_C'])
print(df[df['temperature_C']>22])

lessons.title: Opening a file with NumPy
lessons.goal: Read a data table with NumPy.
lessons.body:
The first cell prepares the text file for this exercise. np.loadtxt reads it back as an array. skiprows=1 skips its first line, which describes the columns.

With unpack=True, the three columns are assigned to X, Y1 and Y2. The last cell displays the data that have been read back to check the result.
lessons.code:
# Préparation ajoutée pour rendre l’exemple autonome
import numpy as np
x = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 100)
B = np.column_stack((x, np.sin(x), np.cos(x)))
np.savetxt("tableau.txt",B,header="x sin cos")

B = np.loadtxt("tableau.txt",skiprows=1)

X,Y1,Y2 = np.loadtxt("tableau.txt",skiprows=1,unpack=True)

# Observation complémentaire des données relues
print(B.shape)
print(B[:3])
print(X[:3])
print(Y1[:3])
print(Y2[:3])

lessons.title: Saving a file with NumPy
lessons.goal: Save an array to a text file.
lessons.body:
After array B has been prepared, np.savetxt writes its three columns to tableau.txt. The header parameter provides a header line preceded by # by default.

Without a delimiter parameter, values are separated by spaces. Renaming the file with a .csv extension does not change its separator. The last cell reads the first lines of the created file to check that it has been written correctly.

In Basthon, this file is in Python’s file space; writing it does not, by itself, download it to your computer.
lessons.code:
# Préparation ajoutée pour rendre l’exemple autonome
import numpy as np
x = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 100)
B = np.column_stack((x, np.sin(x), np.cos(x)))

np.savetxt("tableau.txt",B,header="x sin cos")

# Observation complémentaire du fichier créé
with open("tableau.txt",encoding="utf-8") as fichier:
    for i in range(4):
        print(fichier.readline().rstrip())

lessons.title: Normal distribution and spread of measurements
lessons.goal: Understand the normal distribution and the spread of measurements.
lessons.body:
A normal distribution is described by its mean μ and its standard deviation σ. Its density is p(x) = exp[−(x−μ)2/(2σ2)] / (σ√(2π)).

The code compares a histogram normalised using density=True with this theoretical density. It distinguishes the spread of the measurements, estimated by s, from the standard uncertainty of their mean due to repeatability, estimated by s/√N for independent measurements.

Approximately 68 % of the values in a normal distribution lie between μ−σ and μ+σ. This is the proportion of individual values, not a confidence interval for the mean. The code estimates this proportion in the sample.
lessons.code:
# Exemple complémentaire : simuler des mesures et décrire leur dispersion
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
mu=10.0
sigma=0.5
N=10000
a=np.random.normal(mu,sigma,N)
m=a.mean()
s=a.std(ddof=1)
u_m=s/np.sqrt(N)
print('Moyenne :',m)
print('Écart-type expérimental :',s)
print('Incertitude-type de la moyenne :',u_m)
print('Fraction à moins de sigma de mu :',np.mean(np.abs(a-mu)<=sigma))
x=np.linspace(mu-5*sigma,mu+5*sigma,500)
p=np.exp(-0.5*((x-mu)/sigma)**2)/(sigma*np.sqrt(2*np.pi))
plt.hist(a,bins=50,density=True,label='Mesures simulées')
plt.plot(x,p,label='Densité normale')
plt.xlabel('Valeur mesurée')
plt.ylabel('Densité de probabilité')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

lessons.title: Removing columns with Pandas
lessons.goal: Remove columns by name or position.
lessons.body:
df.drop removes a row or a column. Here, axis=1 refers to columns and inplace=True modifies df directly.

The four examples use either column names or their positions in df.columns. Each example starts from a copy of the same table so that previous deletions do not affect the next one. An inspection cell displays the remaining columns after each deletion.
lessons.code:
# Préparation ajoutée : tableau de démonstration
import pandas as pd
df_initial = pd.DataFrame([[1,2,3,4,5,6]], columns=['column_name','column_name1','column_name2','d','e','f'])

# Préparation ajoutée : repartir du tableau initial
df = df_initial.copy()

#drop one column by name
df.drop('column_name', axis=1, inplace=True)

# Observation complémentaire après suppression
print(df.columns.tolist())
print(df)

# Préparation ajoutée : repartir du tableau initial
df = df_initial.copy()

#drop multiple columns by name
df.drop(['column_name1', 'column_name2'], axis=1, inplace=True)

# Observation complémentaire après suppression
print(df.columns.tolist())
print(df)

# Préparation ajoutée : repartir du tableau initial
df = df_initial.copy()

#drop one column by index
df.drop(df.columns[[0]], axis=1, inplace=True)

# Observation complémentaire après suppression
print(df.columns.tolist())
print(df)

# Préparation ajoutée : repartir du tableau initial
df = df_initial.copy()

#drop multiple columns by index
df.drop(df.columns[[0,2,5]], axis=1, inplace=True)

# Observation complémentaire après suppression
print(df.columns.tolist())
print(df)
